title: Other Tongues and a Famine of the Word
english: “For eye,” it says, “has not known, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). Then he shows what kind of affliction will come upon them first: “through contempt of lips,” he says, “and through another tongue” (Isaiah 28:11).

This is the meaning of the prophecy. In the Acts of the holy apostles it is written that “on the day of Pentecost they were all gathered together in one place, and behold, there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty wind rushing” (Acts 2:1-2). Then it says: “There appeared to them tongues dividing, as of fire, and it sat upon each one of them, and they began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:3-4).

For Christ had commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, until they should be clothed with power from on high (Acts 1:4; Luke 24:49). Then they went down and spoke to those of Israel, and to all who had come from other countries, in the tongues given them by God; “and those who heard were amazed, and indeed said: Look, are not all these who are speaking Jews? And how do we each hear them speaking in our own tongue? But others said,” it says, “They are full of new wine” (Acts 2:7-8, 13), that is, they are drunk.

This, I think, is the “through contempt of lips, through another tongue.” For they spoke in other tongues, and the God who can do all things had foretold this too: “In other tongues,” he says, “and with the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they believe” (1 Corinthians 14:21). They ought to have accepted the sign as full proof, bearing in mind the prediction God had made about it. This they did not do; instead they mocked the apostles as drunk and remained in disobedience.
“For they will speak to this people, saying to it: This is the rest for the one who drinks, and this is the ruin; and they would not hear” (Isaiah 28:12).

God once said, angered at the madness of the Jews: “Behold, I am bringing a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord. And from the east to the west they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it” (Amos 8:11-12).

So a spiritual famine has been brought upon those of Israel. Since they did not receive through faith the bread of life that came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33), they have quite fittingly come to lack the food that God gives: “For man shall not live by bread alone,” it says, “but by every word that comes out of the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3).
They behaved outrageously toward the Savior and Redeemer of all; yet because He is good, He called Israel to repentance, though it had been impious beyond bearing…

title: Vain Comfort, and Ariel Besieged
english: …“Take counsel; exalt a vain comfort” (Isaiah 28:29).

Having promised them amnesty for their drunken outrages, and having said very plainly that He will not be too harsh with them, He bids them lay hold of good counsel. But He rebukes them because they thought a vain comfort to be something great and lofty, and so were carried beyond what is reasonable. And what was this comfort which they held to be great, though it brought no profit? Surely that one. For they said: “We have made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death; if a rushing storm passes through, it will not come upon us; we have made a lie our hope, and by the lie we shall be sheltered” (Isaiah 28:15).

But those who pondered these things and held an empty hope, supposing that they would die before the calamities came, heard plainly: “If a rushing storm comes upon you, you will be trampled down by it. Whenever it passes by, it will take you” (Isaiah 28:18-19).

“Woe, city of Ariel, which David besieged! Gather produce year upon year, for you will eat with Moab. For I will afflict Ariel, and her strength and her wealth will be Mine. And I will encircle you like David, and set a palisade around you, and set towers around you; and your words will be brought low to the earth, and your words will sink into the earth. And your voice will be like those who speak from the earth, and your voice will grow faint toward the ground” (Isaiah 29:1-4).

He takes up something that happened in history in the time of the reign of blessed David, and he does this as if to bring to light what the synagogue of the Jews dared to do against Christ. For the things that befell the people of old as in shadows are types of the true things.

Now the present Jerusalem was once called Jebus. Blessed David besieged it, and for what cause we shall learn from the holy Scriptures themselves. For it runs thus in the Second Book of Samuel: “And David and all his men went to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite who inhabited the land; and it was said to David, David shall not come in here; for the blind and the lame rose up, saying, He shall not come in here. And David took the stronghold of Zion; this is the city of David. And David said on that day: Let everyone who strikes a Jebusite attack with the dagger the blind and the lame, who fight against the life of David” (2 Samuel 5:6-8).

So the blind and the lame from Jerusalem, or Jebus, opposed blessed David, and for doing this they perished miserably; for he took the city. And at the time of His coming, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, lame and blind, opposed Christ, the Savior of all; for they did not know how to walk uprightly. title: Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt
english: …“to a people who will not profit them, neither for help nor for profit, but for shame and reproach” (Isaiah 30:5).

Again he laments over those from Israel as lovers of sin who have become apostates, exceedingly wicked and planning bitter things, not through God (Isaiah 30:1). For it is not right for those who wish to agree together on some evil thing to take counsel with God. But everyone who is pious and good and a lover of righteousness will take counsel with God and will go on to do what must be done. For it is written: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Proverbs 12:5).

He therefore accuses chosen Israel of bringing in, concerning Christ, a mind out of tune with God. For they deliberated, sitting in council, and indeed said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away both your city and your country.” And another, one of those set among the leaders, says: “You know nothing at all; it is better that one man should die, and not that the whole nation should perish” (John 11:47-50).

The Lord teaches this very thing more clearly in the parables of the Gospel: “The master of the house who planted the vineyard sent his own servants to receive the fruits, but the tenants killed them” (Matthew 21:33-35). And the charges of their impiety did not stop there; for when they saw the son, sent by the father after the servants, they said among themselves, it says: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him and have his inheritance for ourselves” (Matthew 21:38).

So the authors of such bitter and unholy schemes are apostates, who add sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1). For they killed, as I said, the holy prophets, and after them the heir himself, that is, the Son. And he tries to show that their mind had long been turned toward apostasy from God, saying: “Those who set out to go down into Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and to be sheltered by the Egyptians” (Isaiah 30:2). He threw in the words “but they did not ask Me” in between.

The train of thought runs like this: Woe, he says, to those who go down into Egypt to be helped by Pharaoh and to find shelter from the Egyptians. For when war and battle had been announced to them, and the king of Assyria had taken up arms against the land of the Jews, they ran ahead to the Egyptians and called for their help. Yet they ought to have appeased God and, by turning to better ways, to have wiped away the offences by which they had struck against Him. For had they been rich in His favor, they would not have fallen under the feet of those making war…
